title: Great Britain household shopping absorbs shortages through extra cost, substitution and search effort
source_unit: UK Office for National Statistics, Public opinions and social trends, Great Britain: personal experiences of shortages of goods, 5 to 30 August 2026
geography: Great Britain; adults aged 16 years and over living in private households

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; food-shopping experience in the prior two weeks

denominator.unit: responding adults aged 16+ in the ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey item

spent_more.unit: percent saying they had to spend more than usual to get what they normally buy

less_variety.unit: percent reporting less variety in shops than usual

more_shops.unit: percent saying they had to go to more shops than usual

online_substitution.unit: percent saying they had to shop online to get what they normally buy

observations.method: ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey, weighted estimates with published 95% confidence intervals; multiple responses were permitted.
observations.uncertainty: The survey measures self-reported experiences in a two-week window; it does not identify causes, price amounts, food quality, household income, transaction records or duration beyond the question period.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults aged 16 years and over; the workbook also provides age, sex and other breakdowns.
observations.counterinterpretation: Spending more can reflect price changes, product choice, quality substitution or one-off shopping conditions; more shopping can be voluntary as well as scarcity-driven.

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; food-shopping behaviour in the prior two weeks

denominator.unit: responding adults aged 16+ in the ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey item

buying_less.unit: percent saying they were buying less

buying_more.unit: percent saying they were buying more

habits_unchanged.unit: percent saying shopping habits had not changed

room_conversion.value: shortage and price pressure coexist with unchanged habits for many and reduced purchasing for a substantial minority

observations.method: ONS weighted survey estimates; responses were collected over 5 to 30 August 2026.
observations.uncertainty: Buying less is not separated into lower quantity, cheaper products, healthier or less healthy substitution, reduced waste, or unmet need; the estimates are not causal.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults aged 16 years and over.
observations.counterinterpretation: Unchanged shopping habits may reflect stable access, successful adaptation, or inability to reduce essential purchases; it should not be treated as unchanged household welfare.

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; products unavailable or inaccessible

denominator.unit: responding adults aged 16+ in the ONS Opinions and Lifestyle Survey item

essential_food_unavailable.unit: percent reporting essential food items they needed regularly were unavailable or inaccessible

other_food_unavailable.unit: percent reporting other food items were unavailable or inaccessible

medicine_unavailable.unit: percent reporting medicine was unavailable or inaccessible

fuel_unavailable.unit: percent reporting fuel was unavailable or inaccessible

everything_available.unit: percent saying everything they needed had been available

observations.method: ONS weighted survey estimates from the personal-experiences-of-shortages workbook; question wording includes goods that respondents could not buy or access because they were not available.
observations.uncertainty: The measure does not establish whether an item was unavailable at all stores, unaffordable, medically substitutable, delayed, or ultimately obtained; the wording changed from May 2026 to include access and new response options.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults aged 16 years and over.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported unavailability may reflect local stock, timing, choice, transport or affordability, not only a national supply shortage.

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; source and comparability boundary

denominator.unit: ONS dataset publication and time-series frame

comparison_boundary.value: the ONS warns that question wording and response options changed from 6 to 31 May 2026, limiting comparison with earlier availability estimates

observations.method: ONS spreadsheet with current cross-sectional tables, time-series tables, weighted counts, sample sizes and 95% confidence intervals.
observations.uncertainty: Comparisons across the wording break should not be interpreted as a single uninterrupted trend; different item bases and response structures also matter.
observations.subgroup: Great Britain adults aged 16 years and over.
observations.counterinterpretation: The current estimates remain useful for exposure and adaptation at the August 2026 window even when historical comparability is limited.

related_sources.claim: ONS Excel workbook containing current tables, subgroup estimates, time series, weighted counts, sample sizes and confidence intervals.

boundary: This record adds a household-material conversion route: goods availability and food-shopping friction become extra spending, more search, online substitution, buying less and possible unmet need. It is a weighted ONS survey window, not transaction data, a price index, a supply-chain diagnosis, a food-security measure, or a causal estimate. Question wording changed in May 2026 for the availability item, limiting historical comparisons.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The ONS dataset landing page, August 2026 workbook, cover sheet, notes, current tables and time-series tables were reviewed for sample frame, food-shopping friction, purchasing behaviour, unavailable goods, confidence intervals and the May 2026 wording break.
